items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to the adoption subsidies
provided for disabled or hard to place children
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8745

SPONSOR: PERSAUD
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the social services law, in relation to the adoption
subsidies provided for disabled or hard to place children

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

Relates to the subsidies that may be provided to a parent to who adopts
a disabled or hard to place child.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill amends paragraph (c) of subdivision 1 of section
453 of the social services law and adds three new paragraphs (c-2),
(c-3), and (c4). These provisions provide parameters for the termination
of an adoptive parent's adoption subsidy payments and their subsequent
transfer to the child or new guardian in cases where the parent no long-
er provides direct support or loses their parental rights. Provided,
however, that a guardian who previously lost their parental rights to
whom a child returns would be ineligible to receive an adoption subsidy.

Section 2 of the bill amends clause (b) of subparagraph (iii) of para-
graph (g) of subdivision 1 of section 453 of the social services law to
entitle a child to retroactive direct payment of subsidy payments where
the twenty-first birthday of the child occurs while awaiting the certif-
ication of a representative payee and assistance to the adoptive parent
or parents was terminated pursuant to paragraph (c-2) of the subdivi-
sion.

Section 3 of the bill amends subdivision 2 of section 453 of the social
services law to specify that any agreement provided for in subdivision 1
of the section shall be subject to the approval of the department upon
the application of the social services official in accordance with
applicable regulations.

Section 4 of the bill sets the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

New York State Social Services Law Section 453 assists, in the form of a
monthly subsidy, to help adoptive parents meet the varied and often
costly needs of children who are adopted out of foster care. These
subsidy payments* are made to the adoptive parents of children who fall
within the definition of "handicapped" and "hard to place."  Payments
can total up to $1,941 per month per adopted child and continue until
the child's twenty-first birthday. In New York State, 97.8 percent of
parents who adopt children from foster care receive the adoption subsi-
dy.

Most adoptive parents use the subsidy as it was intended for the bene-
fit, support, and care of the adopted children in a permanent, safe,
stable, and loving home. In some cases, however, the subsidy is paid to
adoptive parents who are neither providing a home nor support for his or
her adopted child. A number of these are instances in which the children
have returned to foster care (on voluntary placement, abuse or neglect
charges, PINS petitions). In 2015, the New York City Administration for
Children's Services ("ACS") confirmed this to be the case. Then-Commis-
sioner Gladys Carrion reported that in a single month during the previ-
ous year ACS had paid the adoption subsidy for 143 adopted children who
were, at the time of payment, back in foster care.

The Commissioner's statistic, which she deemed "alarming," does not
fully capture the extent of the problem, as it only accounts. For
payments made within New York City and does not include cases in which a
court granted custody or guardianship to another adult (due to the
inability or unwillingness of the adoptive parent to continue to care
for the child), or cases in which the children find themselves forced to
live on their own before turning 21. Notably, the latter results in many
young people becoming homeless or suffering from housing instability.

Notwithstanding the intent of the adoption subsidy to benefit the child,
NYS law currently contains no provision for the social services district
paying the subsidy to confirm that the adoptive parent is, in fact,
supporting his or her adopted child. The law also contains no provision
that authorizes courts to suspend, terminate or reduce the adoption
subsidy, or to order that the subsidy be transferred from the adoptive
parent to another individual who is caring for the child. Currently, the
adoption subsidy may be paid to a successor custodian/guardian or the
adoptee, directly, only when the adoptive parent dies. This bill is
necessary to ensure that the subsidy flows to a successor guardian or
custodian, and ultimately benefits the adopted child, in all cases in
which an adoptive parent is no longer providing a home or support for
the child.

This bill is also necessary to ensure that the State is not paying the
subsidy to an adoptive parent and at the same time providing support for
the child through another system - such as foster care, SNAP ("food
stamps"), cash assistance, or shelter placement because the adoptive
parent is not using the subsidy for the care and support of the child.
Enacting this bill to prevent duplicative payments could result in
substantial savings to the State. At any given point in time, there are
at least 150 children in New York City, alone, who has reentered foster
care after adoption. The State is simultaneously paying the adoption
subsidy and the foster care subsidy for these children. Eliminating this
double payment could save a minimum of $12 million.

This bill will ensure that in NYS the adoption subsidy is linked to each
adopted child and permit the subsidy to be transferred if an alternate
adult receives a final order of custody or guardianship for the child.
It will also provide a means for the subsidy to be given directly to
youth or to a payee who has been certified by a local DSS to help the
young person manage the subsidy payments when he or she is over the age
of 18 and no longer receives support from an adoptive parent. Without
unnecessary disruption to families or inappropriate intrusion into fami-
ly life, this Act safeguards funds that the State provides to adoptive
parents to ensure that their adoptive children thrive.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2021-2022: S4055 - Referred to Children and Families

2019-2020: S3562 (Montgomery) - Referred to Children and Families


2017-2018: S6518 (Avella) - Referred to Children and Families; reported
and recommitted to Rules

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately; provided, however, that OCA
shall submit to the United States Department of Health and Human
Services, Administration for Children, Youth and Families, an amendment
to the state title IV-E state plan regarding the provisions of this act
and, not withstanding any other provision of law, this act shall not
take effect unless and until ninety days following the date that the
United States Department of Health and Human Services, Administration
for Children, Youth and Families approves a title IV-E state plan amend-
ment regarding the provisions of this act.

summary: Authorizes the social services department to terminate the subsidies that may be provided to a parent who adopts a disabled or hard to place child under certain circumstances.
